introFa: کتاب «Musicophilia: Tales of Music and the Brain» نوشته Oliver Sacks یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Musicophilia: Tales of Music and the Brain»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: WHAT DO MUSICAL CHAIRS AFFORD? 285 “a special class of composers and performers, with the rest of us often reduced to passive listening” (Sacks, p. 244). Clarke similarly bemoans the “sharp di- vision of musical labor (specialist composers, performers, and listeners), and the listening style with which it has become entwined : : : ” (Clarke, p. 205). Sacks suggests that at concerts, music festivals, and church services, listeners may become involved in active listening; yet in these communal situations, in which music fulﬁlls its “primary function” and “primal role,” there can be only one response: Music is “not only heard but internalized, identically, in all who are present. Rhythm turns listeners into participants, makes listening active and motoric, and synchronizes the brains and minds : : : of all who participate” (Sacks, pp. 244–245). Sacks invokes neurogamy, a state similar to the hive- mind or collective consciousness, in which experience ceases to be unique to the individual. From his vantage point, when musical listening is at its most “active,” the listener is stripped of agency. Clarke criticizes the very venues (the cathedral and concert hall) that Sacks applauds, suggesting that the formal concertgoing experience interrupts or suspends the perception–action cycle. He cites this as a cultural phenomenon speciﬁc to the Western “high art” tradition and notes other popular and traditional cultures and contexts in which “active participation is the norm” (Clarke, p. 20). Although Clarke and Sacks differ on where active musical listening takes place, both characterize listeners as having no innate ability to control or direct their experiences of music. Context and culture determine the response. With an agenda to reactivate musical listening within Western culture, Sacks and Clarke hope to show how music matters and what it means. Yet they hold fast to the characterization of music as an imposed stimulus whose perception is mediated by outside factors. They concur with dominant musical-psychological research paradigms asserting that acquired knowledge “out there” is prerequisite to the meaningful experience of music “in here” and that supplemental repre- sentations grant meaning and purpose to perception (Krumhansl, 2001; Meyer, 1967; Narmour, 1990). Such enrichment-based approaches assume that auditory sensation and musical perceptions are relatively meaningless and that “percep- tion really only becomes musical when it is in relation to events, sequences, progressions and structuring in memory” (McAdams, 1987, p. 23). For Sacks it is the mind, and for Clarke, the culture, that gives meaning to the otherwise meaningless experience of sound and environment. Ways of Listening is the more ambitious offering. Clarke intends to show how the musical environment involves not only the stuff of music (the abso- lute work of art) but also the stuff of the listener’s mind: the biases, predis- positions, and contextual factors contributing to the interpretation of musical affordances: “how different attributes of the perceived meaning of this music— relating to sound, structure, and ideology—coexist and are simultaneously avail- able” (Clarke, p. 10). To this end, chapter 1 (“Perception, Ecology, and Music”) Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

286 NONKEN presents an introduction to ecological theory, which considers how adaptation, perceptual learning, affordances, and invariants function in musical contexts, also exploring the roles of nature and culture and drawing parallels to con- nectionist theory. Chapters 4 and 5 (“Music, Motion, and Subjectivity” and “Autonomy/Heteronomy and Perceptual Style”) examine engagement and how the subject-position (a term, borrowed from cultural and ﬁlm studies, referring to the purposive attitude of the perceiver) may inﬂuence information pickup. These chapters are interspersed with musical analyses. Unlike those found in most musical journals, these analyses are designed to elucidate how the listener interprets the elements of the musical environment; one, for example, presents a schematic representation of three related domains of perceptual meaning, refer- ring to factors that specify “instability in the sound,” “instability in the musical material,” and “unstable or mutually antagonistic cultural practices” (Clarke, p. 60). Full chapters are devoted to Jimi Hendrix’s Woodstock performance of “The Star-Spangled Banner” and Beethoven’s String Quartet, op. 132. Other examples include Haydn, Mozart, Stravinsky, Berg, Zappa, Fatboy Slim, and PJ Harvey. Reacting to cognitive and psychoacoustic studies of measurable musical materials (acoustic information) positing universally perceived musical structures, Clarke orients the discussion toward the experience of the individual listener. As a musical analytical study, Clarke’s book makes some compelling points, but as an application of ecological principles, it is less convincing. A serious problem is its tendency to equate percepts and concepts. Perceptual and concep- tual meanings can be distinguished from one another in terms of how precisely their meaning-boundaries can be speciﬁed. A property that affordances and concepts share is that instances of either can have multiple meanings; however, there are differences in the ways each manifests this property. In the case of affordances, multiple perceptual meanings stem from the multiple functions an object can serve: : : : The multiple meanings of concepts are far less limited because use does not constrain their possibilities. Even though concepts may be ultimately derived from perception–action experience : : : they can become detached and autonomous from everyday realities. It is this characteristic that gives concepts their great creative power, such as can be seen in the arts. (Heft, 2001, p. 131) This distinction has signiﬁcant implications. Percepts and concepts coexist in musical experience, and processes of perception and conception direct the dis- crimination of contextual meaning. Yet Clarke’s perception and conception (in- terpretation) are inseparable. His semiotic bias and insistence that musical per- ception is not only about sounds but also about the meanings they specify for a given listener lead him “beyond the conﬁnes of the music itself—to a world of physical actions and bodily movement, other musical styles, dramatic or narrative Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

WHAT DO MUSICAL CHAIRS AFFORD? 287 context, ideological allegiances, commercial considerations, gender, politics” (Clarke, pp. 126–127). He drifts toward conception: social construction, associ- ation, enculturation, and imagination. “Culture and ideology are just as material (in the concreteness of the practices that embody them) as are the instrument and human body,” he maintains, “: : : and, as perceptual sources, they are just as much a part of the total environment” (Clarke, p. 61). Ultimately, he concedes that musical listening offers listeners the experience of “‘impossible worlds’ : : : [affording] peculiarly direct insight into a limitless variety of subjective experiences of motion and embodiment—real and virtual” (Clarke, p. 90). Like Sacks, he hints at the otherworldly. With an ever-decreasing correlation between stimulation and precept, however, his application of ecological principles and use of the term “environment” are highly metaphorical. Ecological psychology is concerned with the awareness and activities of organisms in a vital, living environment. This is not the amorphous landscape Clarke describes. In this musical virtual reality, the functional quality of the affor- dance is obscured. Moreover, it loses its original sense of usefulness. Clarke char- acterizes the affordance broadly, writing that “the ﬁrst movement of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony affords writing (or speaking about): : : : Music affords dancing, singing (and singing along), playing (and playing along), working, persuading, drinking and eating, doing aerobics, taking drugs, playing air guitar, traveling, protesting, seducing, waiting on the telephone, sleeping : : : the list is endless” (Clarke, p. 204). Surely, this is more a list of things to do while listening than a description of direct perception, and it appears to be about anything but the mu- sic. If we accept that music speciﬁes seduction or comment, we must also accept a highly expanded idea of what speciﬁcation means in the ecological context. The objective quality of the affordance and subjective nature of interpretation are the live components in ecological perception. The position and orientation of the perceiver determine what is perceived, how, and why. In introducing the idea of the affordance, Gibson described the physical world at length, rigorously detailing its mutual relation to the organism; its materials, substances, and surfaces; and the opportunities for perception afforded (Gibson, 1966, pp. 7– 30). Yet the musical environment is part of this world and its perception just as direct. There is no reason to maintain that the arts exist in a virtual environment. In rare statements considering the subjective nature of aesthetic perception, Gibson (1966) depicted the experience and perception of art as involving the same psychological mechanisms as everyday perception and no less based in reality (p. 62). In private correspondence dated August 22, 1970, to Norman Malcolm, his colleague in the philosophy department at Cornell University, he characterized musical listening as indelibly connected to sensory exploration. Responding to a question presumably asking what listeners do when they hear different things in the same music, and referring to his past work (Gibson, 1966, p. 248), he replied, Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

288 NONKEN “the same stimulus array” will always afford the same perceptual experience insofar as it carries the same variables of structural information: : : : I would argue that structural sequence of sounds may in fact be music, 18th century music, Mozart, badly played Mozart, a sonata, etc. All of them are in the structure of the sounds. When a listener “hears” one rather than another, he does not detect a difference in the structure for the different perception, he only abstracts different features of the available structure. I do not mean that he detects different structures in each case. Structure, in sound and light, is inexhaustibly rich. Gibson’s conception of musical listening as an active, direct engagement with the musical material opposes those of Sacks and Clarke, who minimize the importance of the perceiver’s interaction with musical structures. As described earlier, Gibson’s active musical perception resembles the autonomous musical hearing (“the closed world of ‘purely musical sounds’”) that Clarke deems passive. Yet to Gibson, the material itself is rich, offering an inﬁnite world of sensation apart from the also stimulating enrichment offered by abstract thought. Perhaps realizing that his application of the terms “affordance” and “envi- ronment” is metaphorical, Clarke writes, A reader might object that this discussion : : : is unacceptably speculative, full of interpretive license, and basically out of step with an ecological approach: it seems to depend heavily on verbal and dramatic information to interpret the perceptual information : : : rather than relying on speciﬁcation by stimulus invariants. But this overlooks the fact that all of the elements mentioned (the drama, the characters, the sounds) are part of the available information for a viewer/listener. (Clarke, p. 88) In this extension of ecological theory, cultural factors are directly speciﬁed in the auditory invariants of music. So long as information (sensory or conceptual) is “available,” its perception is equally direct. Distinctions between perception and conception, and real and virtual environments, are not accepted. Clarke cites the psychoacoustician Bregman: “Experiences of real sources and of virtual sources : : : are different not in terms of their psychological properties, but in the reality of the things that they refer to in the real world” (Bregman, 1990, p. 460), maintaining that, regardless of the reality or virtual reality of an object or event, the psychological process is identical. Cultural conventions, “arbitrary though they may be in principle, are in practice as binding as a natural law” (Clarke, p. 47). One may wonder to which natural law Clarke refers and how this directs the agency of the perceiver. That aside, within an ecological theory, it is problematic that the environment be so broadly conceived. It brings into question what the affordance is good for and what perception actually is. Unlike Clarke, Sacks does not apply ecological principles to the musical experience. He is interested in the physiological and neurological processes Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

WHAT DO MUSICAL CHAIRS AFFORD? 289 that accompany musical experiences; in addition to sensory, real-time musical listening, these include performances, memories, hallucinations, and imagined experiences. Musicophilia is divided into four sections: “Haunted by Music,” which considers patients suffering from musical obsession, seizures, musico- genic epilepsy, and musical hallucinations; “A Range of Musicality,” which examines amusia and dysharmonia as well as the abilities of savants, synaes- thetics, and the blind; “Memory, Movement, and Music,” which focuses on therapeutic uses of music in the contexts of amnesia, aphasia, Tourette’s syn- drome, Parkinson’s disease, and musicians’ dystonia; and “Emotion, Identity, and Music,” which explores how music and musicality inﬂuences personality, with particularly interesting descriptions of depressives and those with Williams syndrome. He adheres to a traditional simulus-response model of perception, so Musicophilia cannot be considered in any way an endorsement of ecological theory. However, the case studies presented, seen in the light of ecological psychology, suggest compelling avenues for future research. Sacks acknowledges that in listening to music, basic mechanisms developed in the course of everyday perceptual learning are at play. Genuine stereo perception, either visual or auditory, depends on the brain’s ability to infer depth and distance : : : a spatial disparity in the case of the eyes, a temporal disparity in the case of the ears. Tiny differences are involved here, spatial disparities of a few arc seconds with vision, or of microseconds with hearing. This allows some animals : : : to construct a veritable sound map of the environment. We humans are not up to this standard, but we nevertheless use binaural disparities, no less than visual cues, for orienting ourselves, for judging or forming impressions of what lies around us. (Sacks, p. 144) However, the processes involved in judging and forming impressions of the musical environment are missing from Sacks’s view. He embraces the physical, describing the sites of neurological damage and cerebral mechanisms (the acti- vation of various regions of the brain, as evidenced by MRIs, and the coincident ﬁring of neural transmitters). When faced by a situation inexplicable by phys- ical evidence, in which music is shown to stimulate part of the brain thought inaccessible or produce an unexpected activity, he turns to poetic description, unable to explain “the overwhelming, and at times, helpless, sensitivity of our brains to music” (Sacks, p. 45). The perceiver’s orientation within the musical environment, capacities for discrimination, and processes of perceptual learning remain unexplored. The listener is depicted as a mere receptor of acoustic information. Despite his stated belief in the active nature of musical listening, Sacks’s language furthers the impression of a passive subject upon whom the stimulus is imposed. As case studies show, music’s effects can be dramatic. It may return language to those for whom it has been lost and restore memory to the amnesiac. It Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

290 NONKEN may bring awareness to the torpid and trigger violent seizures in the otherwise calm. This seems extraordinary. Yet music is no miracle but an experience available to everyone. Reducing the mental function to a purely material pro- cess and coating it with a spiritual veneer, Sacks effectively quashes what is distinctively psychological about musical listening. By not recognizing the everyday, “ordinary” processes of perception involved in his patients’ growth, Sacks is relegated to extolling music as a near-magical stimulus. His emphasis on preacquired knowledge and schematic representations leads him to wonder if near-supernatural forces are at work when brain-damaged patients, who have lost certain capacities for memory and abstract thought, engage enthusiastically and meaningfully with music. “The power of music,” he writes, “whether joyous or cathartic, must steal on one unawares, come spontaneously as a blessing or a grace” (Sacks, p. 299). But is this really the power of music at work? Music’s restorative power may reside in the processes of perceiving and perceptual learning. Interaction with the sound environment and the processes involved in attending to and discriminating its materials may be responsible for its transformative effects. To entertain this notion, however, one must accept the listener as an active seeker of information, not a passive receiver. Sacks does not do this. Instead, he minimizes the importance of immediate perception, maintaining that the mind exercises control over all basic percepts: “Perception : : : has to draw on experience of the past: : : : We all have detailed memories of how things have previously looked and sounded, and these memories are recalled and admixed with every new perception” (Sacks, p. 148). Perception without the mediation of the fully functioning “musical brain” is impoverished and dysfunctional. When a disabled subject engages with music in an unanticipated way, Sacks (unscientiﬁcally) judges it miraculous, not attributable to the patient’s goals and needs but to music’s awesome power. A case in point is that of Rachel Y., a composer and pianist who, after a traumatic car accident, suffered auditory simultagnosia (the inability to dis- criminate general sounds in the auditory environment) and dysharmonia (the inability to conceptualize harmonic and pitch relations and integrate different voices and elements in a musical texture). She also suffered problems of visual synthesis and physical paralysis and permanent deafness in her left ear. After the accident, Rachel was unable to compose, listen, and perform as before; despite her extensive training and best efforts, she was unable to return to her previous way of conceiving music. “: : : In a way I hear too much,” she stated. “I absorb everything equally: : : : It is extremely difﬁcult to integrate all these different voices into some entity that makes sense” (Sacks, p. 113). Thirteen years later, her brain remained damaged, and the massive physical injury had resulted in permanently lost access to certain kinds of representational knowledge. Yet she had returned to composing and learned to play the piano again. Having developed new interests in painting and photography, she was creating a multimedia piece Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

WHAT DO MUSICAL CHAIRS AFFORD? 291 that brought together elements of her original artworks (visual and musical) and performance. Sacks depicts Rachel’s situation as particularly tragic and can only laud her “reconciliation and acceptance” (Sacks, p. 119). Rachel’s case is a powerful example of perceptual learning. Her perceptual systems suffered a debilitating blow. Yet despite her altered cognitive and sensory capacity, she learned anew how to effectively discriminate the affordances of the environment and reestablished her relation to the world of colors, images, and sounds. Although not recovering her previous conceptual knowledge, she developed new ways, practically and aesthetically, of relating physical, visual, and auditory sensation. Sacks hints at this, suggesting that how she learned to deal with her visual and auditory simultagnosia inﬂuenced her creative work: “She would notice one thing, then another, then a third, her attention would be commandeered successively by different elements, and she would piece the scene together as a whole only slowly: : : : Her paintings and collages made use of this weakness and, indeed, turned it into a new strength, disassembling the visual world and reassembling it in new ways” (Sacks, p. 117). Sacks’s grammatical constructions—passive—reveal his tendency to see perception sim- ilarly. Rachel’s attention was not “commandeered” but directed. Her paintings and collages did not turn her weakness into strength; rather, she learned to direct and retrain her attention and to make art that reﬂected her experience of the world. Rachel’s case suggests that aesthetic and everyday perception are closely related and that perception is not just a mental affair but a skill learned, exploratory and voluntary. Her transformation is not the result of her remembering more or recovering what she lost but evidence of her strength and discipline. Rachel’s progress cannot be explained within the stimulus-response paradigm, to which Sacks clings even when it does not serve his argument. He cannot begin to examine these learning processes so long as he remains committed to the perception of music as a mediated re-presentation of experience. In an attempt to justify how incoming stimuli are perceived and interpreted by the mind, in top-down and bottom-up fashion simultaneously (prefaced as something that might seem “preposterous”), he writes, : : : there are massive efferent connections : : : going from the brain to the cochlea and thence to the outer hair cells. The outer hair cells : : : calibrate or “tune” the inner hair cells, and they have an exclusively efferent nerve supply; they do not transmit nerve impulses to the brain, they get orders from the brain. Thus one has to see the brain and ear as forming a single functional system, a two-way system, with the ability not only to modify the representation of sounds in the cortex but to modulate the output of the cochlea itself. The power of attention : : : is very remarkable and seems to depend on this ability to modulate cochlear function: : : : (Sacks, p. 137) Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

292 NONKEN This introduction of a two-way system is presented in the context of Jacob L., an older composer and conductor suffering hearing loss and distortion due to a deteriorating cochlea. In certain registers, Jacob heard some pitches as sharper, and some ﬂatter, than they actually were; the nature of the pitch distortions was inconsistent in different registers (ranging from a slight microtonal inﬂection to the width of a major third) and changed on a daily basis. For more than a year, he attempted to exercise efferent control over his cochlea, to use his conscious mind to force his ear to learn to rehear these pitches. His attempts were largely unsuccessful, although Sacks attests to being impressed by Jacob’s ability to retrain his ear “by attention or will : : : and, in more general terms, by musical activity.” As his patient left him, he wondered, “Could this musical brain not compensate for and transcend the aberrations of a damaged cochlea?” but expressed conﬁdence because the composer “knew how music : : : should sound. It was only his perception of music that was distorted” (Sacks, pp. 137– 141). A few years later, Jacob reported that his condition had dramatically improved, evidently as the result of immersing himself in a challenging project that involved composing a work for string orchestra in a dissonant, twelve-tone language. He wrote, “This improvement seemed to start happening right after I was composing, producing, conducting, and trying to hear : : : harmonically and texturally complex music with an extremely wide tonal range : : : I was gradually strengthening whatever mechanism of will exists in the old gray matter that can be focused on this problem.” Sacks responds, “And I, as a neurologist, am ﬁlled with wonder : : : that through intensive musical activity, attention and will, Jacob’s brain has literally reshaped itself” (Sacks, p. 144). Neural chemistry and circuitry may be reshaped through musical activity, but the brain does not reshape itself. We may more fruitfully see this as a case of a man teaching himself to attend in new ways, adapting his changed perceptual apparatus to a novel musical environment. Jacob was an active perceiver and his actions self-determined. That an organism whose sensory system was hindered by a damaged component (the deteriorated cochlea) would learn to rediscrimi- nate pitches is remarkable. Within an ecological framework, however, it is not the cause of wonder. Sacks is unwilling to acknowledge the learning process and the reality of its consequences. We can examine one more case, that of Jorgen Jorgenson. Having lost all hearing in his right ear after the removal of an acoustic neuroma (a noncancerous tumor on the nerve connecting the ear to the brain), he had lost his ability to hear in stereo. An avid musical listener, he was distressed by hearing music in “mono” and over time developed a way to hear in “pseudostereo,” with just one ear. In ecological terms, Jorgenson sharpened his ability to discriminate the affordances of the environment, possibly attending more closely to not only acoustic but also visual and spatial information and modifying his physical stance to enhance his visual, auditory, and spatial perceptions. WHAT DO MUSICAL CHAIRS AFFORD? 293 of differentiation, he became increasingly sensitive to distinctions within the musical environment to which he had not been attuned. This resulted in his perceiving more. Like Rachel and Jacob, Jorgenson actively made use of the information available to him in the environment, reﬁning his own perceptual apparatus, however diminished from its previous state. “What is remarkable in Dr. Jorgenson’s case,” writes Sacks, “: : : is that, after such a severe loss, with no possibility of function being restored in the ordinary sense, there has nonetheless been a signiﬁcant reconstruction of function, so that much of what seemed irretrievably lost is now available to him again” (Sacks, p. 142). Although the doctor identiﬁes this reconstructed perceptual function with “the power of cerebral plasticity,” we can also see this as evidencing the strength of the perceptual system, highly adaptable and teachable even when components of the sensory organs are damaged or missing. From a physiological perspective, one might suggest that Jorgenson’s bad right ear was incapable of providing him the information requisite for dimensional hearing. Yet, as Reed (1988) has written, active perceivers are driven to obtain the information they desire from the “boundless” stimulation offered by the environment. “The information itself is neither good nor bad,” he writes, “except insofar as it can facilitate active awareness and adaptive behavior” (p. 192). In Clarke’s view, the world of music, although experienced like real, is virtual. To Sacks, music is an intangible, mystical force. Both support the presumably unreal, illusory nature of aesthetic experience. A realist view of the aesthetic experience is offered by Stoffregen (1997), who has discussed ecological psychology in relation to ﬁlm theory. Building on Gibson’s writings, Stoffregen asserts that art offers not illusory experiences but experiences in which perceivers explore depictions, recognized as such, part of the larger sensory environment. Film is not perceived as reality, just as a radio drama, a stage play, or the performance of a mime are not perceived as reality. All of these depicted are perceived for what they are. There is no illusion of reality because there is no illusion at all. (p. 168) Although his research concerns the visual arts, his argument is compellingly applied to auditory perception and music. Just as the perception of the visual arts draws on the perceptual systems we develop navigating the visual and physical environment, musical perception draws upon the skills and strategies developed in daily auditory perception. As ﬁlm offers a depiction of physical events framed by the camera, reproduced before our eyes, a musical work offers a nested acoustic environment, one created (through a performance or recording) for our ears. Our drive is to orient ourselves to this new environment, which presents an opportunity for sensory exploration. This directed exploration can have as Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

294 NONKEN its goal simple understanding, and, once we accept that sensory exploration is gratifying in and of itself, we can reconsider behaviors previously assumed to be purely observational (passive), such as the perception and appreciation of art. (Stoffregen, 1997, p. 171) Following this argument, music provides (through a performance or recording) an auditory environment to be explored. Resulting from input of the composer (if there is one) and performer, music offers the ear myriad affordances and structures of which the perceiver’s experience entails guided exploration (inﬂuenced by the artists’ choices) and self-directed exploration. Admiring the famous shower scene from Hitchcock’s Psycho, Stof- fregen comments on the images shown and withheld. “How effective this is in stimulating the imagination! It is this power of limiting and guiding perception that is behind the ﬁlm’s ability to manipulate the viewer” (Stoffregen, 1997, p. 174) What is given and withheld, in music, determines what we listen for next. The musical context offers a situation in which the listener is surrounded by acoustic information. Designed intentionally for sensory exploration, the musical environment is characterized by the presence of not only harmony and rhythm but also such factors as silence, timbre (instrumentation), dynamic (amplitude), density, texture, gestural and motivic ﬁgures, patterns, and audible processes of accretion and degradation (such as crescendi or ritardandi, the processes of getting louder or slower). These factors are affordances, objective characteristics of the music subjectively discriminated in context. To different listeners, they may suggest attending to the music in particular ways, and different works have different parametric proﬁles. In a Bach fugue, a genre designed to showcase the interaction of rigorously structured thematic materials and contrapuntal processes, the listener may be drawn to follow the developments of the subject and countersubject, focusing on the interweavings of polyphonic lines. In John Cage’s 4’33”, a work consisting of four and half minutes in which the musicians are tacet (not playing their instruments at all), listeners may instead ﬁnd themselves newly aware of the environmental sounds that inevitably break the silence. Some musics are rhythmically active and vibrant (such as African drumming or Steve Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians), whereas others focus on the linear aspects of melody (the famous habanera aria “L’amour est un oiseaux rebelle” from Bizet’s Carmen). The various affordances of musical materials and structures remain to be further explored. Regardless of style, different musical works offer unique and highly stimulating opportunities for guided perception. As Clarke and Sacks recognize, musical environments are designed for ex- ploration. It is why we are drawn to them. It is why even those with damaged sensory systems are drawn to them: because of the opportunities for sensation that they provide. Through musical interaction, we learn to discriminate with greater precision, becoming more sensitive to the inexhaustibly rich environ- ment of sound, time, and space. This is a promising area for research, with implications for psychological and musical scholarship. By studying how our perceptual systems engage in musical listening, we may be led to a more nuanced Downloaded by [TOBB Ekonomi Ve Teknoloji] at 19:00 21 December 2014

WHAT DO MUSICAL CHAIRS AFFORD? 295 understanding of perceptual learning. For this to happen, however, we must recognize the real and active aspects of musical listening for what they are. Although not suggesting that musical experience has no connection to abstract thought and contextual factors, we must recognize that perception is driven ﬁrst and foremost not by political ideology, societal forces, or magic but by the desire to experience and understand.
